a: Ignatius, also called Theophorus
p: Every letter opens with the same second name: Theophorus, 'God-bearer'.
b: Greek Theophoros, 'God-bearer'. Lake's footnote to the first letter tells the story of the third-century Acts of Ignatius: asked who Theophorus is, Ignatius answers, 'He who has Christ in his heart.' See the note at Ignatius to the Romans 1:0.

a: Tralles in Asia
p: A rich city on the road east from Ephesus, beyond Magnesia.
b: Lightfoot follows Strabo: 'After leaving Magnesia the road leads to Tralles', about seventeen or eighteen miles on, on the high road 'trodden by all who make the journey from Ephesus to the East'. The city stood on a plateau with steep sides above the Maeander valley and was wealthy; Strabo says the Asiarchs, the presidents of the games, were often taken from its citizens, and the Asiarch at Polycarp's death, Philip, was a Trallian (Martyrdom of Polycarp 12:2; 21:1). Lightfoot: 'This epistle however contains the earliest notice of Christianity in connexion with Tralles.'
r: Martyrdom of Polycarp 12:2; Martyrdom of Polycarp 21:1

a: in the apostolic manner
p: Greek charaktēr, a stamp: Ignatius greets them in the style of an apostle's letter.
b: Greek en apostolikō charaktēri, 'in apostolic stamp'. The charaktēr is the stamp on a coin (Ignatius to the Magnesians 5:2). Lake: 'after the apostolic fashion'. Ignatius greets them the way the apostles greeted churches, with grace and peace (Romans 1:7), while saying in 3:3 that he will not give orders 'like an apostle'. 'In the fullness' (en tō plērōmati): Lake, 'in the Divine fulness'; Lightfoot, 'in the pleroma, the sphere of the Divine graces'. Lightfoot sets aside the other explanations, among them Zahn's 'in the fulness of Christian good wishes', as 'excluded by the use of the word or by the grammar of the sentence'.
orig: ἐν τῷ πληρώματι ἐν ἀποστολικῷ χαρακτῆρι

a: who is our hope in our resurrection into him
p: Christ is 'our hope', a title Ignatius gives him again and again.
b: Greek tēs elpidos hēmōn en tē eis auton anastasei. The title comes from 1 Timothy 1:1, 'Christ Jesus our hope'. Ignatius uses it in 2:2 and in Ignatius to the Magnesians 11:1. 'Into him' points to the resurrection as being raised into union with Christ, as 9:2 says.
orig: τῆς ἐλπίδος ἡμῶν ἐν τῇ εἰς αὐτὸν ἀναστάσει

a: Polybius, your overseer
p: Tralles sent only its overseer to Smyrna.
b: Lightfoot: Ephesus and Magnesia sent several delegates, but Tralles, 'as being more distant, was content with sending a single representative, its bishop Polybius'. Eusebius names him too, as the man 'who was its ruler then' (archōn, Church History 3.36.5). Lightfoot holds that 'these were not fictitious personages' (The Christian Ministry, page 50). 'Overseer' (episkopos) is the word behind 'bishop'.

a: not as a habit but by nature
t: Not by habit but by nature
p: Their goodness is not put on; it is who they are.
b: Greek ou kata chrēsin alla kata physin, 'not by use but by nature'. Lake: 'not from habit, but by nature'. Ignatius means that their steadiness is not borrowed or occasional. 'Unwavering' (adiakriton) is the word Lake cites to explain Ignatius to the Magnesians 15:1.
orig: οὐ κατὰ χρῆσιν ἀλλὰ κατὰ φύσιν

a: in him I saw your whole congregation
t: The whole church in one man
p: As at Magnesia, Ignatius sees the whole church in its overseer.
b: Greek hōste me to pan plēthos hymōn en autō theōreisthai. Ignatius says the same of the Magnesian delegates (Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1) and of Onesimus at Ephesus (Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:3). For him an overseer is the church's face, so that meeting him is meeting them. Lake prints the Greek manuscript's theōreisthai, a middle form, and translates 'I saw'; the long recension has the active theōrēsai, 'to see', which Lightfoot prints: 'There seems to be no good authority for the middle'. The English is the same on either reading (see the variant).
orig: ὥστε με τὸ πᾶν πλῆθος ὑμῶν ἐν αὐτῷ θεωρεῖσθαι
r: Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:3

a: imitators of God
p: Paul: 'be imitators of God, as loved children'.
b: Greek mimētas ontas theou. Paul writes, 'So become imitators of God, like children who are loved' (Ephesians 5:1). Ignatius greets the Ephesians the same way (Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:1).

a: living not in a human way, but in the way of Jesus Christ
p: To be subject to the overseer is, for Ignatius, to live Christ's way.
b: Greek ou kata anthrōpon zōntes, alla kata Iēsoun Christon. Paul asks the quarreling Corinthians, 'are you not living by human ways?' (1 Corinthians 3:3, kata anthrōpon). Lightfoot quotes this line in The Christian Ministry: those 'live a life after Christ' who 'obey the bishop as Jesus Christ'.
orig: οὐ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον ζῶντες, ἀλλὰ κατὰ Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν

a: as to the apostles of Jesus Christ
p: As in Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1, the elders stand for the apostles.
b: Greek tō presbyteriō hōs tois apostolois Iēsou Christou. Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 4:1, where Paul calls himself and Apollos 'assistants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries'. Ignatius sets the council of elders in the apostles' place, as in 3:1 ('the band of the apostles') and Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1.
orig: τῷ πρεσβυτερίῳ ὡς τοῖς ἀποστόλοις Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ

a: deacons of the mysteries of Jesus Christ
p: The deacons serve Christ's mysteries; Paul calls himself a steward of 'God's mysteries'.
b: Greek diakonous ontas mystēriōn Iēsou Christou. 'Mysteries' (mystēria) in Paul are God's plan, once hidden and now made known (1 Corinthians 4:1; Ephesians 3:9). The Greek manuscript has the singular, 'of the mystery'; the long recension and all the versions have the plural, which Lake and Lightfoot print (Lightfoot's apparatus). Ignatius does not say what the deacons' mysteries are; Lightfoot: such a restriction to the Supper 'would be an anachronism in Ignatius', who uses the word as Paul does, 'revealed truths'. Whether the word already means the church's rites, as it later did in Greek, cannot be shown from this verse; the next sentence, 'not deacons of food and drink', suggests the deacons' work at the church's meals was more than serving food.

a: they are not deacons of food and drink
t: Not deacons of food and drink
p: The Seven of Acts 6 were chosen to 'serve tables'. Ignatius says deacons serve the church of God.
b: Greek ou gar brōmatōn kai potōn eisin diakonoi. The Twelve said, 'It is not good for us to set aside the word of God in order to serve tables' (Acts 6:2), and chose seven to do it. Ignatius's deacons are more than table servants: they are 'assistants of the church of God' (hypēretai, the word of 1 Corinthians 4:1, 'assistants of Christ'). Whether the Seven were the first deacons, and what a deacon is today, is the card at Acts 6.
orig: οὐ γὰρ βρωμάτων καὶ ποτῶν εἰσιν διάκονοι

a: let everyone respect the deacons as Jesus Christ
p: Here the deacons, not the overseer, stand for Christ.
b: Greek entrepesthōsan tous diakonous hōs Iēsoun Christon. In Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1 the overseer is 'in the place of God' and the deacons hold 'the ministry of Jesus Christ'; here the deacons are respected 'as Jesus Christ', the overseer as 'a type of the Father', the elders as 'God's council'. The Son of Man, who 'did not come to have people serve him. He came to serve' (Mark 10:45), is the deacon's pattern. Roberts and Donaldson's English reads 'as an appointment of Jesus Christ', the sense of the Latin's ut mandatum iesu christi, 'as a command of Jesus Christ'. Lightfoot rejects that reading 'as standing alone against all the others' and explains it as a blend of two readings (see the variant).
orig: ἐντρεπέσθωσαν τοὺς διακόνους ὡς Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν

a: a type of the Father
p: Greek typos: the overseer is a living picture of the Father to the church.
b: Greek ton episkopon onta typon tou patros. Typos is a stamp, model or picture (Romans 5:14, 'a figure of the one who was coming'); the site writes 'type' here and in Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:2, so the reader sees one word. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it: 'the bishop is typos tou Patros: he is like the living image of God the Father' (Catechism 1549). 'Type' is the reading of the Syriac and the long recension; the Greek manuscript and the Latin read 'Son of the Father', which Lightfoot says 'must certainly be rejected in favour of τύπον' (see the variant). In Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1 two witnesses read 'type' where Lake reads 'place' (see the variant there).

a: Without these, it is not called a church
t: 'Without these it is not called a church': how the churches read it
p: Catholic teaching quotes this sentence; the other churches' documents answer the question it raises without naming Ignatius.
b:
Greek chōris toutōn ekklēsia ou kaleitai. Catholic: the Catechism quotes the verse: 'For without them one cannot speak of the Church' (Catechism 1554). The documents below do not name Ignatius; they answer the question he raises, what makes a church and which ministers it must have. Orthodox: the Orthodox Church in America's The Orthodox Faith: 'the bishops, priests and deacons give order to the Church'. Anglican: the 1662 Ordinal: 'from the Apostles' time there have been these Orders of Ministers in Christ's Church; Bishops, Priests, and Deacons'. Lutheran: the church is where 'the Gospel is rightly taught and the Sacraments are rightly administered', and for its unity 'it is enough to agree concerning the doctrine of the Gospel and the administration of the Sacraments' (Augsburg Confession VII). Reformed: 'Unto this catholic visible church Christ hath given the ministry, oracles, and ordinances of God' (Westminster Confession 25.3). Baptist: a church's officers 'are bishops or elders, and deacons' (Second London Confession 26.8).

Lightfoot's judgment is on the chapter page. See the card on the church in Ephesians and the cards at Acts 20:28 and 1 Timothy 3.

a: his gentleness is power
p: Lake translates 'whose meekness is a miracle', with 'is his power' as another possibility.
b: Greek hē de praotēs autou dynamis. Dynamis is 'power', and in the Gospels also a 'mighty work'. Lake chose 'whose meekness is a miracle' and footnoted: 'Or, possibly, "is his power."' The Plain English Translation takes the plainer sense. Ignatius praises the same gentleness in himself in 4:2: by it 'the ruler of this age is brought down'. Paul appeals 'by the meekness and gentleness of Christ' (2 Corinthians 10:1).

a: even the godless respect him
p: Lightfoot: 'the godless' are the heathen; Christians were called 'atheists' too.
b: Greek tous atheous. Lightfoot: here 'the heathen, who were ἄθεοι ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ' ('without God in the world', Ephesians 2:12). He notes the turn of the word: pagans called Christians atheoi because they had no images, as the crowd shouts at Polycarp in Martyrdom of Polycarp 9:2, and in 10:1 Ignatius uses it of the teachers who deny Christ's suffering.

a: that I, a condemned man, should give you orders like an apostle
p: Ignatius will not command as an apostle: he is a condemned man.
b: Greek hina ōn katakritos hōs apostolos hymin diatassōmai. He says the same to Rome: 'I am not commanding you as Peter and Paul did. They were apostles; I am a condemned man' (Ignatius to the Romans 4:3), and to Ephesus, 'I do not command you as though I were someone' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 3:1). The sentence is badly damaged in the manuscripts (see the variant).
orig: ἵνα ὢν κατάκριτος ὡς ἀπόστολος ὑμῖν διατάσσωμαι
r: Ignatius to the Romans 4:3; Ignatius to the Ephesians 3:1

a: Those who talk to me that way are whipping me
p: Flattery is a scourge to a man about to die for Christ.
b: Greek hoi gar legontes moi mastigousin me, 'those speaking to me scourge me'. Lake: 'For they who speak thus are a scourge to me'. Ignatius means those who praise him and so tempt him to pride. Lightfoot names this clause among the places in these chapters where 'the state of the text' is not sound, but Lake prints it without a note. Paul was given 'a thorn ... in the flesh' 'to keep me from lifting myself too high' (2 Corinthians 12:7).
orig: οἱ γὰρ λέγοντές μοι μαστιγοῦσίν με

a: the jealousy is not seen by many
p: Lake: 'the jealousy of the devil'; or, he notes, 'Ambition is not obvious'.
b: Greek to gar zēlos pollois men ou phainetai, eme de pleon polemei. Lake translates 'the jealousy of the devil is to many not obvious' and footnotes: 'This is probably the meaning: an alternative translation would be: "Ambition is not obvious, etc." But cf. the letter to the Romans v. 3', where Ignatius prays, 'May nothing seen or unseen envy me' (Ignatius to the Romans 5:3). On the first reading the devil's jealousy fights the martyr; on the second, Ignatius's own eagerness to die. Lightfoot takes the first, 'the jealous opposition of Satan, who attempts to rob me of the crown of martyrdom', noting that the long recension adds 'of the enemy' after 'jealousy'; of the second he says that Ignatius 'would consider such a passion as the reverse of blameworthy'. The site renders zēlos 'jealousy' in these books, as in 1 Corinthians 13:4.

a: the ruler of this age is brought down
p: The devil is defeated not by force but by gentleness.
b: Greek en hē katalyetai ho archōn tou aiōnos toutou. 'The ruler of this age' is Ignatius's name for the devil, from Paul's 'rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing' (1 Corinthians 2:6). Here it is gentleness that undoes him, as Christ won by suffering.
orig: καταλύεται ὁ ἄρχων τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου

a: since you are infants
p: Paul fed the Corinthians milk, 'as infants in Christ'.
b: Greek nēpiois ousin hymin. Paul: 'I ... could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as people made of flesh, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food' (1 Corinthians 3:1-2). Lake's margin reference is unclear on his page: one scan reads '1 Cor. 3, 1. 2', the other and the digital text '8, 1. 2'. Hebrews 5:12-13 has the same picture. Ignatius's point is not that the Trallians are slow but that heavenly things can harm those not ready for them.

a: the places of the angels and the gatherings of the rulers, seen and unseen
p: Lake's margin: Colossians 1:16, 'the seen and the unseen, whether thrones or lordships or rulers'.
b: Greek tas topothesias tas angelikas kai tas systaseis tas archontikas, horata te kai aorata. Paul says that in Christ were created 'the seen and the unseen, whether thrones or lordships or rulers or authorities' (Colossians 1:16). Ignatius claims to understand the arrangement of the heavenly powers, but says it does not make him a disciple: what counts is reaching God. Lightfoot calls topothesiai 'the dispositions' of the angels, their places, and systaseis 'the assemblages, musterings, of the heavenly rulers'.
orig: τὰς τοποθεσίας τὰς ἀγγελικὰς καὶ τὰς συστάσεις τὰς ἀρχοντικάς

a: am not already a disciple because of that
p: Knowledge does not make a disciple; only reaching God does.
b: Greek para touto ēdē kai mathētēs eimi, with the 'not' of the start of the verse. Ignatius says in Ignatius to the Romans 5:3, 'Now I am beginning to be a disciple', and in Ignatius to the Ephesians 3:1. Paul: 'Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up' (1 Corinthians 8:1).
orig: παρὰ τοῦτο ἤδη καὶ μαθητής εἰμι

a: the foreign weed, which is heresy
p: Heresy is a weed that does not belong in the church's food.
b: Greek allotrias de botanēs apechesthe, hētis estin hairesis. Lightfoot: heresy is called a botanē, 'a rank weed, a noxious herb', again in Ignatius to the Ephesians 10:3 ('weed of the devil') and To the Philadelphians 3:1. 'Heresy' (hairesis) is the term of Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:2; in the New Testament the word is still 'faction' (Galatians 5:20). 'Not I but the love of Jesus Christ' echoes Paul's 'But it was not I; it was the grace of God that is with me' (1 Corinthians 15:10).
orig: ἀλλοτρίας δὲ βοτάνης ἀπέχεσθε, ἥτις ἐστὶν αἵρεσις
r: Ignatius to the Ephesians 10:3; Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:2; Galatians 5:20; 1 Corinthians 15:10; Matthew 15:13

a: a deadly poison mixed with honeyed wine
p: Like a poisoner, the false teacher hides the drug in a sweet drink.
b: Greek thanasimon pharmakon didontes meta oinomelitos. Oinomeli is wine mixed with honey. Lightfoot collects the same picture in Theophilus, Lactantius and Ephrem, and notes that the poisoners were 'mimicking genuine physicians', who hid bitter medicine in sweet drinks. Paul warns of those who 'With smooth words and flattering talk ... fool the hearts of the unsuspecting' (Romans 16:18). Contrast Ignatius's own 'medicine of immortality' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2).

a: inseparable
p: The Greek may mean 'from God, Jesus Christ' or 'from our God Jesus Christ'; the Armenian lacks 'God'.
b: Greek achōristois theou Iēsou Christou. Lake: 'inseparable from God, from Jesus Christ'; his footnote: 'Or possibly "from our God Jesus Christ"', and on the Greek: 'The text is doubtful. A omits θεοῦ: probably there is some corruption though it is impossible to be sure what it is.' Lightfoot prints 'God' in brackets and writes: 'Probably this word should be omitted with the Armenian Version. Though Ignatius frequently speaks of Jesus Christ as God, it may be questioned whether he ever so styles Him without some explanatory or qualifying phrase.' If it is kept, he says, it 'should perhaps be separated from' Christ ('of God, of Jesus Christ'), though the missing 'and' is 'hardly consistent with the genius of the Greek language'. Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2 has such a phrase: 'our God, Jesus the Christ'. Here 'God' stands alone. The Plain English Translation keeps the words as Lake prints them, with no comma.

a: the ordinances of the apostles
p: Greek diatagmata: the apostles' instructions, as 'the decrees of the Lord and of the apostles' in Magnesians.
b: Greek tōn diatagmatōn tōn apostolōn. Ignatius to the Magnesians 13:1 has 'the decrees of the Lord and of the apostles'. Lightfoot quotes this line in The Christian Ministry among the letters' strongest phrases. Ignatius does not say what the ordinances were; Paul hands on 'traditions' by word and letter (2 Thessalonians 2:15).
r: Ignatius to the Magnesians 13:1; 2 Thessalonians 2:15; 1 Corinthians 11:2

a: Whoever is within the altar is pure
p: Lake translates 'sanctuary'; the word is 'altar', as in Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2.
b: Greek ho entos thysiastēriou ōn katharos estin. Lake: 'He who is within the sanctuary is pure'. The site keeps 'altar' for thysiastērion in all the letters, so the reader sees the one word: 'If anyone is not within the altar, he goes without God's bread' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2), and 'one altar' (Ignatius to the Magnesians 7:2). Ignatius explains himself at once: to be outside the altar is to do anything 'without the overseer, the council of elders and the deacons'. The Greek manuscript lacks 'but whoever is outside the altar is not pure', which the Latin has and the long recension has in a shorter form; Lightfoot puts the loss down to the eye passing between the two clauses that end alike (see the variant). Hebrews: 'We have an altar' (Hebrews 13:10).
r: Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2; Ignatius to the Magnesians 7:2; Hebrews 13:10

a: faith, which is the flesh of the Lord
t: Faith the flesh, love the blood
p: Ignatius turns the body and blood into faith and love.
b: Greek en pistei ho estin sarx tou kyriou, kai en agapē, ho estin haima Iēsou Christou. Lightfoot reads the neuter 'which' (ho) as a whole idea: faith and love are what flesh and blood are to the body. Ignatius pairs faith and love everywhere (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:1, 'The whole thing is faith and love'), and elsewhere says the thanksgiving 'is the flesh of our Savior' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1). Here the words are a picture of the believer's life, not of the Supper; churches that read Ignatius on the Supper are on the cards at Matthew 26:26 and John 6.
orig: ἐν πίστει ὅ ἐστιν σὰρξ τοῦ κυρίου, καὶ ἐν ἀγάπῃ, ὅ ἐστιν αἷμα Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
r: John 6:56; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1

a: It is not that I know of anything of this kind among you
p: As at Magnesia, Ignatius says the Trallians are not yet touched by the teaching.
b: Lightfoot: 'He acquits the Trallians indeed of any complicity in this heresy hitherto, but he writes to put them on their guard.' He notes that this letter, unlike To the Magnesians, makes 'no allusion' to 'the Judaic side of the heresy'. Compare Ignatius to the Magnesians 11:1.

a: Woe to the one through whom my name is insulted for no reason among some
p: Lake's margin: Isaiah 52:5, which Paul quotes in Romans 2:24. Ignatius's form is his own.
b:
Greek Ouai gar, di' hou epi mataiotēti to onoma mou epi tinōn blasphēmeitai. The Greek Isaiah 52:5 (Swete) reads 'Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations'; Paul quotes it, 'as it is written, "The name of God is insulted among the Gentiles because of you"' (Romans 2:24). The site's Isaiah 52:5, from the Hebrew, ends 'my name is treated with contempt'.

Ignatius's words are none of these: he begins with 'Woe', adds 'for no reason' and 'among some', and turns it on the one person whose conduct brings shame. Lightfoot counts it among the three formal quotations of the Old Testament in the seven letters, though here there is no 'it is written'. The Plain English Translation follows Ignatius's Greek and uses 'insulted', the site's word in Romans 2:24, for blasphēmeitai.
orig: Οὐαὶ γάρ, δι᾽ οὗ ἐπὶ ματαιότητι τὸ ὄνομά μου ἐπί τινων βλασφημεῖται

a: So be deaf when anyone speaks to you apart from Jesus Christ
p: Ignatius answers the teachers with a list of facts, each marked 'truly'.
b:
Greek Kōphōthēte oun, 'Be deaf, then'. What follows reads like a confession of faith: of David's family (Romans 1:3), of Mary (Galatians 4:4), truly born, eating and drinking, truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate, truly crucified and dead, truly raised by his Father (9:2). Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1-2 and Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2 have similar lists. Lightfoot calls the denunciation of Docetism 'fuller and more explicit in this than in any other of his letters'.

Whether Ignatius is quoting a set formula or using his own words, the text does not say. Lightfoot's paraphrase draws out the point of each clause: 'His human body was no mere phantom. He was really born. He really ate and drank.'
r: Romans 1:3; Galatians 4:4; 1 Timothy 6:13; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1-2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2

a: He was of David's family and of Mary
t: Of David's family and of Mary
p: Ignatius says 'of Mary', not 'of a virgin', here.
b: Greek tou ek genous Daueid, tou ek Marias. 'Of David's family' is Paul's 'came from the offspring of David' (Romans 1:3). 'Of Mary' stresses a real human mother, as Paul's 'born of a woman' (Galatians 4:4). Ignatius speaks of Mary's virginity in Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1 and 'born of a virgin' in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1; this verse says only 'of Mary'.
orig: τοῦ ἐκ γένους Δαυείδ, τοῦ ἐκ Μαρίας
r: Romans 1:3; Galatians 4:4; Matthew 1:16; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1

a: he ate and drank
p: A real body needs food; the risen Jesus ate with his disciples too.
b: Greek ephagen te kai epien. Against those who said his body was only an appearance, Ignatius names ordinary human acts. Peter says of the risen Christ, 'We shared meals with him, eating and drinking, after he rose from among the dead' (Acts 10:41); Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 3:3 says the same.
r: Acts 10:41; Luke 24:42-43; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 3:3

a: in the sight of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth
t: Heaven, earth and under the earth
p: The whole creation watched him die, in the words of Philippians 2:10.
b: Greek blepontōn tōn epouraniōn kai epigeiōn kai hypochthoniōn. Paul's hymn: 'every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth' (Philippians 2:10), with the same three Greek words. Ignatius makes them witnesses of the crucifixion. 'Under the earth' may also point to the dead whom Christ visited (Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:2).
orig: βλεπόντων τῶν ἐπουρανίων καὶ ἐπιγείων καὶ ὑποχθονίων
r: Philippians 2:10; Revelation 5:13; Ignatius to the Magnesians 9:2

a: when his Father raised him
p: Here the Father raises the Son; in Smyrnaeans 2:1 Christ 'raised himself'.
b: Greek egeirantos auton tou patros autou. The New Testament says both: God raised him (Acts 2:24; Romans 10:9; Galatians 1:1) and he takes up his life again (John 10:18). Ignatius too says both: here the Father raised him, and in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1, 'he also truly raised himself'. One scan of Lake prints a comma before this phrase, the other a full stop.
r: Galatians 1:1; John 10:18; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1

a: without whom we do not have true life
p: Paul argues the same way in 1 Corinthians 15: if Christ was not raised, neither will we be.
b: Greek hou chōris to alēthinon zēn ouk echomen. Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 15:12 and following: 'if no resurrection of the dead exists, then not even Christ has been raised' (1 Corinthians 15:13). Ignatius turns it around: because Christ was truly raised, the Father 'will also raise us'. 'True life' answers the teachers who made his life seem unreal.
orig: οὗ χωρὶς τὸ ἀληθινὸν ζῆν οὐκ ἔχομεν

a: he suffered only in appearance
p: Greek to dokein, 'the seeming': the word behind the name docetism.
b:
Greek to dokein peponthenai auton, autoi ontes to dokein. The site writes 'only in appearance' for to dokein, as in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1, and keeps Ignatius's retort, 'they themselves are only in appearance!'. Lake's introduction calls the teaching 'docetism (δοκεῖν), which regarded the sufferings, and in some cases the life, of Jesus as merely an appearance'.

John's test is the same: 'any spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is from God' (1 John 4:2); 'many deceivers went out into the world, people who do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh' (2 John 1:7).
r: 1 John 4:2-3; 2 John 1:7; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1

a: Why do I even pray to fight wild beasts
p: Ignatius's own coming death is the argument: if Christ's suffering was a show, his is pointless.
b: Greek ti de kai euchomai thēriomachēsai. The verb is Paul's: 'As a mere man I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus' (1 Corinthians 15:32), and Paul argues the same way: 'why are we in danger every hour?' (1 Corinthians 15:30). Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 4:2 makes the same point: 'if these things were done by our Lord only in appearance, then I too am in chains only in appearance'.
r: 1 Corinthians 15:30-32; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 4:2; Ignatius to the Romans 5:1

a: the Father's planting
p: Lake's margin: Matthew 15:13, 'Any plant that was not planted by my heavenly Father will be uprooted'.
b: Greek ouk eisin phyteia patros. Jesus: 'Any plant that was not planted by my heavenly Father will be uprooted' (Matthew 15:13), where the Greek for 'plant' is phyteia, Ignatius's word. To the Philadelphians 3:1 uses the same picture. The 'bad offshoots' bear 'deadly fruit', as 'a rotten tree produces bad fruit' (Matthew 7:17).
orig: οὗτοι γὰρ οὔκ εἰσιν φυτεία πατρός

a: branches of the cross
p: The cross is a tree, and true believers are its branches, bearing fruit that does not decay.
b: Greek klados tou staurou. Ignatius makes the cross a tree, as the New Testament calls it 'the tree' (Acts 5:30; 1 Peter 2:24), and the church its branches, near Jesus's 'I am the vine. You are the branches' (John 15:5). Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:2 has the same picture: 'We are from that fruit'. 'By the cross' renders 'through which' (di' hou); it could also mean 'through whom'.
r: John 15:5; Acts 5:30; 1 Peter 2:24; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:2

a: a head cannot be born apart, without members
p: Christ the head and his members belong together: God's promise is union.
b: Greek ou dynatai oun kephalē chōris gennēthēnai aneu melōn. Paul: Christ 'is the head of the body, the church' (Colossians 1:18), and 'we are one body in Christ' (Romans 12:5). Ignatius adds: 'God promises union, which is himself'. Lake: 'The head therefore cannot be borne without limbs', reading 'borne' for 'born'; the Greek gennēthēnai is 'be born'.

a: I greet you from Smyrna
p: The churches gathered round Ignatius at Smyrna join in the greeting.
b: Eusebius: at Smyrna Ignatius wrote to Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles, 'whose ruler then was Polybius', and to Rome (Church History 3.36.5). 'The churches of God that are here with me' are the delegates of Ephesus and Magnesia and the church of Smyrna itself (13:1; Ignatius to the Magnesians 15:1).
r: 13:1; Ignatius to the Magnesians 15:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:1

a: above all for the elders, to refresh the overseer
p: The elders' first duty here is to give their overseer rest.
b: Greek exairetōs kai tois presbyterois, anapsychein ton episkopon. Anapsychō is 'refresh, give breathing room', the word Paul uses of Onesiphorus, of whom he says 'many times he lifted my spirits' (2 Timothy 1:16). Lightfoot quotes this line in The Christian Ministry as showing that the elders 'are not put out of sight'.

a: not be found disqualified
p: Lake's margin: 1 Corinthians 9:27, 'in case I ... am disqualified myself'.
b: Greek hina mē adokimos heurethō. Paul: 'I batter my body and lead it off as a slave, in case I proclaim to others and then am disqualified myself' (1 Corinthians 9:27). Lightfoot: 'The idea of a race seems to be present here'. 'The lot' (klēros) is the share Ignatius hopes for: martyrdom and God.

a: so that my letter does not stand as a witness against you
p: A letter ignored becomes evidence against its readers.
b: Greek hina mē eis martyrion ō en hymin grapsas, 'that I may not, having written, be for a testimony among you'. Lake: 'that I become not by my writing a witness against you'. Moses' song was given so that 'this song will be my witness against the Israelites' (Deuteronomy 31:19).
orig: ἵνα μὴ εἰς μαρτύριον ὦ ἐν ὑμῖν γράψας

a: the last of them
p: Ignatius calls himself the least of Antioch's believers.
b: Greek ōn eschatos ekeinōn. Ignatius says the same in Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:2 ('the last of the faithful there') and Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:1. Paul: 'I am the least of the apostles' (1 Corinthians 15:9).
r: 1 Corinthians 15:9; Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:1

a: gives itself as an offering
p: Greek hagnizetai: 'is made an offering, devoted'. The same word as Ephesians 8:1.
b: Greek hagnizetai hymōn to emon pneuma. Lake: 'my spirit'; Roberts and Donaldson: 'Let my spirit be sanctified by yours'. Lightfoot, on the same verb in Ignatius to the Ephesians 8:1 ('I give myself as an offering for you'), explains it as 'I am devoted to', since hagnizein sometimes means 'to sacrifice'. The site renders it the same way in both letters. Paul: 'I am already a drink offering being poured out' (2 Timothy 4:6).
r: Ignatius to the Ephesians 8:1; 2 Timothy 4:6; Philippians 2:17
